review_notes: Read the whole file and the stieltjesWeight definition and simp lemma in Stieltjes/Basic.lean. Grepped the repo for uses of the inversion lemmas; they are only used inside this file. I did not run Lean, so both findings are about expected simp behaviour. They are not observed failures. The other simp lemmas (`stieltjesInversion_singleton_zero`, `stieltjesInversion_stieltjesInversion_eq_restrict`, `isStieltjesFunction_comp_inv_div_iff`) look sound: each shrinks its term or has a clear normal form.

findings.problem: This iff is a `@[simp]` lemma that expands any `Integrable g (stieltjesInversion μ)` into `Integrable (fun x => (x:ℝ)⁻¹ • g x⁻¹) μ`. The right side is larger, and it hides the `stieltjesInversion` structure. The file's own consumer is the weight lemma `integrable_weight_stieltjesInversion_iff_restrict`, which has the nicer normal form `Integrable stieltjesWeight (μ.restrict {0}ᶜ)`. That lemma is not simp. Once the generic lemma is simp, a `simp` call on the weight goal will probably use the generic lemma first. It would then produce `(x:ℝ)⁻¹ • stieltjesWeight x⁻¹`, which `stieltjesWeight_apply` unfolds further. The two lemmas compete, and the generic one gives the worse form. The file itself uses `rw [integrable_stieltjesInversion_iff]` and never relies on simp for it. Its sibling `integral_stieltjesInversion` is not simp either, so the interface is inconsistent.
findings.proposed_change: Remove `@[simp]` from `integrable_stieltjesInversion_iff`. Mark the specialised `integrable_weight_stieltjesInversion_iff_restrict` as `@[simp]`, or at least keep it as the documented entry point. The proof in that lemma already uses `rw`, so it needs no change. Do the same for `integrable_weight_stieltjesInversion_iff`, which needs the discharger `μ {0} = 0`.
findings.benefit: `simp` on Stieltjes-weight integrability for a transformed measure would reach the intended normal form, the restriction of `μ` to `{0}ᶜ`. It would no longer expand into a `smul` of an inverse composition. Callers would also be less likely to see unexpected goal shapes from this generic rewrite.

evidence.excerpt: lemma stieltjesWeight_apply (x : ℝ≥0) : stieltjesWeight x = (1 + (x : ℝ))⁻¹

findings.excerpt:
theorem representsStieltjes_comp_inv_div_iff {ν : Measure ℝ≥0} {a b : ℝ≥0} {f : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hν : ν {0} = 0) :
findings.problem: This conditional iff is `@[simp]` and its left-hand pattern is `RepresentsStieltjes ν b a (fun t => f t⁻¹ / t)`. It rewrites to `RepresentsStieltjes ν.stieltjesInversion a b f`. Three problems follow. First, simp has to discharge `ν {0} = 0`, which holds only if the caller supplies it. Second, the pattern contains `?f t⁻¹` under a binder, which is not a higher-order pattern. It will match only when the target has a syntactically similar lambda. Third, the right side can match the same rule again when `f` is itself of the form `fun t => g t⁻¹ / t`. Then `stieltjesInversion_stieltjesInversion_eq_restrict` gives `ν.restrict {0}ᶜ`, whose atom-at-zero hypothesis is not syntactically `ν {0} = 0`. The proof of this very lemma works around the competing rule by passing `Measure.stieltjesInversion_stieltjesInversion hν` to `simpa`. The unconditional simp lemma `stieltjesInversion_stieltjesInversion_eq_restrict` would normally rewrite the same term first.
findings.proposed_change: Make the simp interface explicit. Drop `@[simp]` from `representsStieltjes_comp_inv_div_iff` and keep it as a manually applied iff. If a simp form is wanted, add a separate unconditional rule such as `RepresentsStieltjes ν b a (fun t => f t⁻¹ / t) ↔ RepresentsStieltjes ν.stieltjesInversion a b f` for `ν` already of the form `stieltjesInversion _`, or state the rule for `ν.restrict {0}ᶜ`. That removes the side condition and the interaction with the double-inversion rewrite.
findings.benefit: The simp set would have one unconditional normal form for double inversion. Rewriting would no longer depend on a side goal that simp usually cannot discharge, and a repeated application would not produce `restrict` forms that no longer match the hypothesis. Callers would get predictable behaviour from `simp`.
